description:
SpaceMission– Advancing Astronaut Health Through Technology

We are SpaceMission, a team dedicated to developing innovative health monitoring solutions for astronauts during space missions.

Our goal is to design software that tracks vital health indicators, analyzes health data, and helps monitor astronauts' well-being in challenging space environments.

By combining technology, science, and innovation, we aim to contribute to safer and healthier space exploration.
summary: AstroHealth is health monitoring software for astronauts on space missions. It is a web application that tracks the vital signs of a four-person crew in real time, interprets the readings and recommends what to do. The backend is written in Java 21 with Spring Boot; the interface is plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript. The main screen shows the four astronauts as holograms: the selected one moves to the front, and anyone in critical condition glows red. Each body is drawn as a heat map coloured by skin temperature, and the heart area, the warmest point, pulses at the astronaut’s heart rate. Selecting a body part enlarges it and shows its own readings, such as skin temperature and estimated blood flow. An automatic assessment reads heart rate, blood oxygen, temperature, blood pressure, stress and radiation together, names the main finding (for example “Signs of hypoxia”) and lists recommended actions. A crew table compares all four astronauts with the person most at risk at the top, and alerts are raised when a reading crosses its threshold. Radiation risk is calculated from NASA’s open DONKI space weather database, using recent solar flares, geomagnetic storms and particle events. We tried six visual designs before choosing the hologram style, and removed several features to keep the product focused. Vital signs are currently simulated rather than read from real sensors, and the assessment is rule-based, not medically validated.
details:
Project Details

What it does. AstroHealth monitors the health of a four-person space crew in real time. It shows each astronaut’s vital signs, flags readings that leave the safe range, explains what the readings mean together, and recommends what to do next.

How it works. A Java backend generates a new set of readings for every astronaut every two seconds: heart rate, blood oxygen, core body temperature, blood pressure, respiration, stress, sleep, cumulative radiation dose and skin temperature for eleven body regions. Each reading is checked against warning and critical thresholds, and alerts are raised automatically. A rule-based assessment then combines the readings into one finding, such as signs of hypoxia or fever, with a short list of recommended actions.

Interface. The crew appears as four holographic astronauts. Each body is a heat map coloured by skin temperature, and the heart area pulses at the astronaut’s heart rate. Selecting a body part enlarges it and shows its readings. A crew table compares all four astronauts and puts the person most at risk first.

NASA data. Radiation risk comes from NASA’s open DONKI database. The app reads the last 30 days of solar flares, geomagnetic storms and solar energetic particle events, scores them, and turns the score into a risk level that sets how fast the crew’s radiation dose rises.

Benefits. Flight surgeons and crew see one clear picture instead of separate numbers, and problems are explained in plain language with next steps.

Tools. Java 21, Spring Boot, REST API, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, SVG and Canvas.

Limits and next steps. Vital signs are simulated; the next step is connecting real wearable sensors. The assessment rules are simplified and not medically validated.
